measures.name: Everyday executive skills
measures.domain: Executive functioning and ADHD
measures.description: Executive functioning skills, including plan and time management, organization, and emotional and behavioral regulation
measures.licenceNote: Strait et al. (2020) scale, free to use; NovoPsych page carries a NovoPsych copyright notice. Confirm with Dr Peg Dawson or the authors before clearing.
measures.instructions: Read each item and decide how often it's a problem for you.

items.text: I act on impulse.
I say things without thinking.
I lose things.
I have a short fuse.
I get upset when things don't go as planned.
I run out of steam before finishing a task.
It's hard for me to set priorities when I have a lot of things to do.
My desk or workspace is a mess.
I have trouble keeping my house or room clean.
I have trouble estimating how long it will take to complete a task.
I'm slow at getting ready for school, work, or appointments.
If the first solution to a problem doesn't work, I have trouble thinking of a different one.
I skip checking my work for mistakes, even when the stakes are high.
I get annoyed when tasks are too hard.
It's hard for me to put aside fun activities to start things I know I need to do.
I have trouble with tasks where I have to come up with my own ideas.
It's hard for me to tell how well I'm doing on a task.
I have trouble reaching long-term goals.
I "go with my gut" when making decisions.
I get so wrapped up in what I'm doing that I forget about other things I need to do.
Little things frustrate me.
I have trouble getting back on track if I'm interrupted.
I have trouble making a plan.
I miss the big picture.
I live for the moment.

subscales.label: Planning and managing tasks
subscales.strengthReason: You described planning and managing tasks as something that mostly goes smoothly for you.
subscales.focusReason: Planning and keeping track of tasks came up often in your answers.

subscales.label: Managing time
subscales.strengthReason: You told us that keeping to time mostly works for you.
subscales.focusReason: Estimating and keeping to time came up as a difficulty in your answers.

subscales.label: Staying organised
subscales.strengthReason: Keeping things and spaces in order mostly works for you.
subscales.focusReason: Keeping things and spaces in order came up as a difficulty in your answers.

subscales.label: Managing feelings
subscales.strengthReason: You described managing strong feelings as something you handle well.
subscales.focusReason: Managing strong feelings came up as a difficulty in your answers.

subscales.label: Pausing before acting
subscales.strengthReason: Pausing before acting and sticking with a plan mostly works for you.
subscales.focusReason: Pausing before acting and sticking with a plan came up as a difficulty in your answers.

source.citation: Developed by Dr. Peg Dawson (Smart But Scattered Kids). Original citation: Strait, J. E., Dawson, P., Walther, C. A. P., Strait, G. G., Barton, A. K., & McClain, M. B. (2020). Refinement and psychometric evaluation of the Executive Skills Questionnaire-Revised. Contemporary School Psychology, 24, 378-388. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40688-018-00224-x

measures.name: Thinking flexibly
measures.domain: Executive functioning and ADHD
measures.description: Cognitive flexibility - the ability to perceive multiple alternative explanations for life occurrences and human behaviour, generate multiple alternative solutions to difficult situations, and perceive difficult situations as controllable
measures.licenceNote: Dennis and Vander Wal (2010); NovoPsych reproduction carries a NovoPsych copyright notice. Confirm author permission before clearing.
measures.instructions: Please use the scale below to indicate the extent to which you agree or disagree with the following statements.

items.text: I am good at "sizing up" situations.
I have a hard time making decisions when faced with difficult situations.
I consider multiple options before making a decision.
When I encounter difficult situations, I feel like I am losing control.
I like to look at difficult situations from many different angles.
I seek additional information not immediately available before attributing causes to behaviour.
When encountering difficult situations, I become so stressed that I can not think of a way to resolve the situation.
I try to think about things from another person's point of view.
I find it troublesome that there are so many different ways to deal with difficult situations.
I am good at putting myself in others' shoes.
When I encounter difficult situations, I just don't know what to do.
It is important to look at difficult situations from many angles.
When in difficult situations, I consider multiple options before deciding how to behave.
I often look at a situation from different view-points.
I am capable of overcoming the difficulties in life that I face.
I consider all the available facts and information when attributing causes to behaviour.
I feel I have no power to change things in difficult situations.
When I encounter difficult situations, I stop and try to think of several ways to resolve it.
I can think of more than one way to resolve a difficult situation I'm confronted with.
I consider multiple options before responding to difficult situations.

subscales.label: Seeing other options
subscales.strengthReason: You described finding other ways of seeing a situation as something that comes readily to you.
subscales.focusReason: Your answers suggest it can be hard to see other ways of reading a situation.

subscales.label: Seeing situations as workable
subscales.strengthReason: You tend to see difficult situations as ones you can do something about.
subscales.focusReason: Your answers suggest difficult situations can feel outside your control.

source.citation: Dennis, J. P., & Vander Wal, J. S. (2010). The cognitive flexibility inventory: Instrument development and estimates of reliability and validity. Cognitive Therapy and Research, 34(3), 241-253. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10608-009-9276-4

measures.name: Attention and activity
measures.domain: Executive functioning and ADHD
measures.description: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) symptoms in adults, spanning inattentiveness and hyperactivity/impulsivity (including motor and verbal components)
measures.licenceNote: Public domain WHO instrument, freely reproducible for clinical use.
measures.instructions: Please answer the questions below, rating yourself on each of the criteria shown. As you answer each question, select the box that best describes how you have felt and conducted yourself over the past 6 months.

items.text: How often do you have trouble wrapping up the final details of a project, once the challenging parts have been done?
How often do you have difficulty getting things in order when you have to do a task that requires organisation?
How often do you have problems remembering appointments or obligations?
When you have a task that requires a lot of thought, how often do you avoid or delay getting started?
How often do you fidget or squirm with your hands or feet when you have to sit down for a long time?
How often do you feel overly active and compelled to do things, like you were driven by a motor?
How often do you make careless mistakes when you have to work on a boring or difficult project?
How often do you have difficulty keeping your attention when you are doing boring or repetitive work?
How often do you have difficulty concentrating on what people say to you, even when they are speaking to you directly?
How often do you misplace or have difficulty finding things at home or at work?
How often are you distracted by activity or noise around you?
How often do you leave your seat in meetings or other situations in which you are expected to remain seated?
How often do you feel restless or fidgety?
How often do you have difficulty unwinding and relaxing when you have time to yourself?
How often do you find yourself talking too much when you are in social situations?
When you're in a conversation, how often do you find yourself finishing the sentences of the people you are talking to, before they can finish them themselves?
How often do you have difficulty waiting your turn in situations when turn taking is required?
How often do you interrupt others when they are busy?

source.citation: Kessler, R. C., Adler, L., Ames, M., Demler, O., Faraone, S., Hiripi, E., Howes, M. J., Jin, R., Secnik, K., Spencer, T., Ustun, T. B., & Walters, E. E. (2005). The World Health Organization Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS): a short screening scale for use in the general population. Psychological Medicine, 35(2), 245-256. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0033291704002892

measures.name: Knowing your strengths

items.text: Other people see the strengths that I have
I have to think hard about what my strengths are
I know what I do best
I am aware of my strengths
I know the things I am good at doing

subscales.strengthReason: You have a clear sense of what your strengths are.

measures.name: Using your strengths
measures.domain: Strengths knowledge, use and support at work
measures.description: Perceived deployment of one's own personal strengths in daily life, i.e. the extent to which a person actively uses what they do best across situations.
measures.licenceNote: No explicit licence found; CAPP asserts copyright over the scales. Confirm before clearing.
measures.instructions: The following 14 questions ask about your strengths, that is, the things that you can do well or do best.

items.text: I am regularly able to do what I do best.
I always play to my strengths.
I always try to use my strengths.
I achieve what I want by using my strengths.
I use my strengths every day.
I use my strengths to get what I want out of life.
My work gives me lots of opportunities to use my strengths.
My life presents me with lots of different ways to use my strengths.
Using my strengths comes naturally to me.
I find it easy to use my strengths in the things I do.
I am able to use my strengths in lots of different situations.
Most of my time is spent doing the things that I am good at doing.
Using my strengths is something I am familiar with.
I am able to use my strengths in lots of different ways.

subscales.label: Using your strengths
subscales.strengthReason: You described using your strengths often, at work and beyond.
subscales.focusReason: Your answers suggest your strengths do not get much use day to day.

source.citation: Govindji, R., & Linley, P. A. (2007). Strengths use, self-concordance and well-being: Implications for strengths coaching and coaching psychologists. International Coaching Psychology Review, 2(2), 143-153.

measures.name: Confidence in your strengths
measures.domain: Strengths knowledge, use and support at work
measures.description: Perceived self-efficacy (confidence) in one's ability to identify, apply and use one's personal strengths across everyday situations, at work or study, and in pursuit of goals.
measures.licenceNote: Distributed free for practitioner use by PositivePsychology.com; no explicit licence from the authors. Confirm before clearing.

items.text: Use your strengths at work?
Use your strengths without any struggles?
Find ways to apply your strengths in the things you do everyday?
Accomplish a lot using your strengths?
Apply your strengths at work/school?
Use your strengths in many situations?
Use your strengths to succeed?

Use your strengths at any time?
Use your strengths to help you achieve your goals in life?
Practice your strengths in areas where you excel?

subscales.label: Confidence in your strengths
subscales.strengthReason: You feel confident applying your strengths when it counts.
subscales.focusReason: Your answers suggest you are not yet confident putting your strengths to use.

source.citation: Tsai, C.-L., Chaichanasakul, A., Zhao, R., Flores, L. Y., & Lopez, S. J. (2014). Development and validation of the Strengths Self-Efficacy Scale (SSES). Journal of Career Assessment, 22(2), 221-232. https://doi.org/10.1177/1069072713493761

measures.name: Repetitive thinking
measures.domain: Repetitive negative thinking and self talk
measures.description: Repetitive negative thinking (RNT), measured as a content-independent process (applies equally to worry, rumination, or any other form of repetitive negative thought about problems), rather than a specific symptom or diagnostic construct.
measures.licenceNote: Elsevier copyright on the article; no permission statement for practice use found. Confirm before clearing.

items.text: The same thoughts keep going through my mind again and again.
Thoughts intrude into my mind.
I can't stop dwelling on them.
I think about many problems without solving any of them.
I can't do anything else while thinking about my problems.
My thoughts repeat themselves.
Thoughts come to my mind without me wanting them to.
I get stuck on certain issues and can't move on.

My thoughts prevent me from focusing on other things.

Thoughts just pop into my mind.
I feel driven to continue dwelling on the same issue.
My thoughts are not much help to me.
My thoughts take up all my attention.

subscales.focusReason: Thoughts that go round and are hard to stop came up often in your answers.

measures.name: How you talk to yourself

measures.domain: Repetitive negative thinking and self talk
measures.description: Self-criticism and self-reassurance as distinct forms of self-relating that people use when things go wrong: an inadequacy-focused form of self-criticism, a more punitive, self-disgust-based (hated-self) form of self-criticism, and the capacity to be self-reassuring/self-supportive.
measures.licenceNote: Author copyright notice (Gilbert et al., 2004); no explicit practice use grant found. Confirm before clearing.
measures.instructions: When things go wrong in our lives or don't work out as we hoped, and we feel we could have done better, we sometimes have negative and self-critical thoughts and feelings. These may take the form of feeling worthless, useless or inferior etc. However, people can also try to be supportive of themselves. Below are a series of thoughts and feelings that people sometimes have. Read each statement carefully and choose the answer that best describes how much each statement is true for you.

items.text: I am easily disappointed with myself.
There is a part of me that puts me down.
I am able to remind myself of positive things about myself.
I find it difficult to control my anger and frustration at myself.
I find it easy to forgive myself.
There is a part of me that feels I am not good enough.
I feel beaten down by my own self-critical thoughts.
I still like being me.
I have become so angry with myself that I want to hurt or injure myself.
I have a sense of disgust with myself.
I can still feel lovable and acceptable.
I stop caring about myself.
I find it easy to like myself.
I remember and dwell on my failings.
I call myself names.
I am gentle and supportive with myself.
I can't accept failures and setbacks without feeling inadequate.
I think I deserve my self-criticism.
I am able to care and look after myself.
There is a part of me that wants to get rid of the bits I don't like.
I encourage myself for the future.
I do not like being me.

flagItems.note: Follow up with the client directly.

measures.name: What you need to feel at your best

measures.domain: Motivation, self determination and goal pursuit
measures.description: The satisfaction and the frustration of the three basic psychological needs identified in self-determination theory: autonomy, competence and relatedness. The scale distinguishes need satisfaction (the needs being met) from need frustration (the needs being actively thwarted, not merely unmet), prod
measures.licenceNote: Copyright Center for Self-Determination Theory; written permission required for commercial use.
measures.instructions: Below, we ask you about the kind of experiences you actually have in your life. Please read each of the following items carefully. You can choose from 1 to 5 to indicate the degree to which the statement is true for you at this point in your life.

items.text: I feel a sense of choice and freedom in the things I undertake.
Most of the things I do feel like "I have to".
I feel that the people I care about also care about me.
I feel excluded from the group I want to belong to.
I feel confident that I can do things well.
I have serious doubts about whether I can do things well.
I feel that my decisions reflect what I really want.
I feel forced to do many things I wouldn't choose to do.
I feel connected with people who care for me, and for whom I care.
I feel that people who are important to me are cold and distant towards me.
I feel capable at what I do.
I feel disappointed with many of my performances.
I feel my choices express who I really am.
I feel pressured to do too many things.
I feel close and connected with other people who are important to me.
I have the impression that people I spend time with dislike me.
I feel competent to achieve my goals.
I feel insecure about my abilities.
I feel I have been doing what really interests me.
My daily activities feel like a chain of obligations.
I experience a warm feeling with the people I spend time with.
I feel the relationships I have are just superficial.
I feel I can successfully complete difficult tasks.
I feel like a failure because of the mistakes I make.

subscales.label: Feeling free to choose
subscales.strengthReason: You feel free to choose how you live and work.
subscales.focusReason: Your answers suggest you do not feel free to choose how you live and work.

subscales.label: Feeling pushed
subscales.strengthReason: You do not feel pushed into things against your wishes.
subscales.focusReason: Feeling pushed into things came up often in your answers.

subscales.label: Feeling connected
subscales.strengthReason: You feel close to the people who matter to you.
subscales.focusReason: Your answers suggest you are not feeling close to the people who matter to you.

subscales.label: Feeling left out
subscales.strengthReason: You do not feel left out or distant from others.
subscales.focusReason: Feeling left out or distant from others came up often in your answers.

subscales.label: Feeling capable
subscales.strengthReason: You feel capable of what you set out to do.
subscales.focusReason: Your answers suggest you are not feeling capable of what you set out to do.

subscales.label: Doubting yourself
subscales.strengthReason: You do not doubt your ability much.
subscales.focusReason: Doubting your ability came up often in your answers.

source.citation: Chen, B., Vansteenkiste, M., Beyers, W., Boone, L., Deci, E. L., Van der Kaap-Deeder, J., Duriez, B., Lens, W., Matos, L., Mouratidis, A., Ryan, R. M., Sheldon, K. M., Soenens, B., Van Petegem, S., & Verstuyf, J. (2015). Basic psychological need satisfaction, need frustration, and need strength across four cultures. Motivation and Emotion, 39(2), 216-236. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11031-014-9450-1

measures.name: Putting things off
measures.domain: Motivation, self determination and goal pursuit
measures.description: Trait (general) procrastination, i.e. the tendency to voluntarily delay an intended course of action despite expecting to be worse off for the delay. The PPS is a distilled, 12-item unidimensional measure combining items drawn from three earlier procrastination scales (the Decisional Procrastination
measures.licenceNote: Items published under CC BY (Svartdal and Steel, 2017).
measures.instructions: Not stated on source

responseOptions.label: Very seldom or not true of me
Very often true, or true of me

items.text: I delay making decision until it's too late
Even after I make a decision I delay acting upon it
I waste a lot of time on trivial matters before getting to final decisions
In preparation for some deadlines, I often waste time by doing other things
Even jobs that require little else except sitting down and doing them, I find they seldom get done for days
I often find myself performing tasks that I had intended to do days before
I am continually saying 'I'll do it tomorrow'
I generally delay before starting on work I have to do
I find myself running out of time
I don't get things done on time
I am not very good at meeting deadlines
Putting things off till the last minute has cost me money in the past

subscales.label: Putting things off
subscales.strengthReason: Putting things off is not a big feature of how you work.
subscales.focusReason: Putting things off came up often in your answers.

source.citation: Svartdal, F., & Steel, P. (2017). Irrational delay revisited: Examining five procrastination scales in a global sample. Frontiers in Psychology, 8, 1927. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.01927

measures.name: Delaying despite good intentions
measures.domain: Motivation, self determination and goal pursuit
measures.description: Irrational procrastination, i.e. the tendency to delay in a way that is knowingly counterproductive to one's own well-being or efficiency, distinguishing procrastination proper from merely intentional or strategic delay.
measures.licenceNote: Items published under CC BY (Svartdal and Steel, 2017).
measures.instructions: Not stated on source

responseOptions.label: Very seldom or not true of me
Very often true, or true of me

items.text: I put things off so long that my well-being or efficiency unnecessarily suffers
If there is something I should do, I get to it before attending to lesser tasks
My life would be better if I did some activities or tasks earlier
When I should be doing one thing, I will do another
At the end of the day, I know I could have spent the time better
I spend my time wisely
I delay tasks beyond what is reasonable
I procrastinate
I do everything when I believe it needs to be done

subscales.label: Delaying despite good intentions
subscales.strengthReason: You mostly do what you intend to, when you intend to.
subscales.focusReason: Delaying things you meant to do came up often in your answers.

source.citation: Svartdal, F., & Steel, P. (2017). Irrational delay revisited: Examining five procrastination scales in a global sample. Frontiers in Psychology, 8, 1927. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.01927

measures.name: Confidence in handling challenges
measures.domain: Motivation, self determination and goal pursuit
measures.description: Generalized self-efficacy, i.e. a broad and stable sense of personal competence to deal effectively with a variety of stressful or difficult situations, treated as a unidimensional trait rather than task-specific self-efficacy.
measures.licenceNote: Authors grant permission to use and reproduce.
measures.instructions: Not stated on source

items.text: I can always manage to solve difficult problems if I try hard enough.
If someone opposes me, I can find the means and ways to get what I want.
It is easy for me to stick to my aims and accomplish my goals.
I am confident that I could deal efficiently with unexpected events.
Thanks to my resourcefulness, I know how to handle unforeseen situations.
I can solve most problems if I invest the necessary effort.
I can remain calm when facing difficulties because I can rely on my coping abilities.
When I am confronted with a problem, I can usually find several solutions.
If I am in trouble, I can usually think of a solution.
I can usually handle whatever comes my way.

subscales.label: Confidence in handling challenges
subscales.strengthReason: You feel confident you can handle what comes your way.
subscales.focusReason: Your answers suggest you are not feeling confident about handling what comes your way.

source.citation: Schwarzer, R., & Jerusalem, M. (1995). Generalized Self-Efficacy scale. In J. Weinman, S. Wright, & M. Johnston, Measures in health psychology: A user's portfolio. Causal and control beliefs (pp. 35-37). NFER-NELSON.

measures.name: Commitment to your goal
measures.domain: Motivation, self determination and goal pursuit
measures.description: Unidimensional goal commitment, i.e. the degree of attachment to, and determination to reach, a specific goal the respondent has in mind, independent of the goal's difficulty or content.
measures.licenceNote: No licence statement found; paywalled Elsevier article. Confirm before clearing. The form must ask the client to name a goal first.
measures.instructions: Think of the main goal you are working on with Sarah. Answer each statement about that goal.

items.text: It's hard to take this goal seriously.
Quite frankly, I don't care if I achieve this goal or not.
I am strongly committed to pursuing this goal.
It wouldn't take much to make me abandon this goal.
I think this is a good goal to shoot for.

subscales.label: Commitment to your goal
subscales.strengthReason: You are firmly committed to the goal you named.
subscales.focusReason: Your answers suggest your commitment to the goal you named is wavering.

source.citation: Klein, H. J., Wesson, M. J., Hollenbeck, J. R., Wright, P. M., & DeShon, R. P. (2001). The assessment of goal commitment: A measurement model meta-analysis. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 85(1), 32-55.

measures.domain: Motivation, self determination and goal pursuit
measures.description: Adaptive self-regulation in the face of unattainable goals, comprising two related capacities: Goal Disengagement (the ability to withdraw effort and commitment from a goal that can no longer be reached) and Goal Reengagement (the ability to identify, commit to, and pursue new goals after disengagin
measures.licenceNote: Society for Personality and Social Psychology copyright; no permission statement found. Confirm before clearing.
measures.instructions: "If I have to stop pursuing an important goal in my life . . ." This is the generic item stem used for all 10 items in Study 2 and Study 3, quoted verbatim from a footnote to Table 1 of Wrosch et al. (2003), fetched and confirmed in this session. In Study 1, the goal disengagement items only were instead presented against three separate situational stems, one of which is quoted verbatim in the article as: "If it becomes likely that I have to stop pursuing an important goal because I no longer have the opportunity to realize it . . ."

items.text: It's easy for me to reduce my effort toward the goal.
I find it difficult to stop trying to achieve the goal.
I stay committed to the goal for a long time; I can't let it go.
It's easy for me to stop thinking about the goal and let it go.
I think about other new goals to pursue.
I seek other meaningful goals.
I convince myself that I have other meaningful goals to pursue.
I tell myself that I have a number of other new goals to draw on.
I start working on other new goals.
I put effort toward other meaningful goals.

subscales.label: Finding new goals
subscales.strengthReason: When a goal is out of reach you find new ones to pursue.
subscales.focusReason: Your answers suggest it is hard to find new goals when one is out of reach.

source.citation: Wrosch, C., Scheier, M. F., Miller, G. E., Schulz, R., & Carver, C. S. (2003). Adaptive self-regulation of unattainable goals: Goal disengagement, goal reengagement, and subjective well-being. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 29(12), 1494-1508.
